This publication compiles WHO recommendations on maternal health, aiming to provide an accessible resource for WHO staff, policymakers, program managers, and health professionals. It also helps identify gaps to prioritize guideline updates. 9. WHO guidelines are developed following the highest international standards, emphasizing transparency and minimizing bias. The process includes evidence synthesis and quality assessment using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. 10. GRADE categorizes evidence quality as high, moderate, low, or very low, based on the likelihood that further research will change confidence in the effect estimates. Recommendations are formulated by expert groups using structured evidence-to-decision frameworks. 11. Recommendations are classified as strong or conditional. Strong recommendations indicate that the benefits of adherence outweigh the harms. Conditional recommendations are made when there is less certainty about the balance of benefits and harms. 12. WHO recommendations on maternal health include details on the conditions under which they should or should not be implemented, along with evidence quality, recommendation strength, and links to sources. 13. Counseling on healthy eating and physical activity during pregnancy is recommended to prevent excessive weight gain. Balanced energy and protein supplementation are advised in undernourished populations to reduce risks of stillbirths and small-for-gestational-age neonates. High-protein supplementation is not recommended. 14. Daily iron and folic acid supplementation is recommended to prevent maternal anemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth. Weekly supplementation may be considered in specific contexts where daily intake is not feasible. 15. Calcium supplementation is recommended to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia in populations with low dietary calcium intake. Vitamin A supplementation is only recommended in areas with severe vitamin A deficiency to prevent night blindness. 16. Zinc supplementation is recommended only in the context of rigorous research. Multiple micronutrient supplementation, as well as vitamin B6, vitamin E, and vitamin C supplementation, are not recommended for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes. 17. Vitamin D supplementation is not recommended for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes. Pregnant women with high caffeine intake should reduce their consumption to lower the risk of pregnancy loss and low-birth-weight neonates. 18. Full blood count testing is recommended for diagnosing anemia in pregnancy. Where unavailable, on-site hemoglobin testing with a hemoglobinometer is preferred over the hemoglobin color scale. 19. Midstream urine culture is recommended for diagnosing asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy. Where unavailable, on-site midstream urine Gram-staining is preferred over dipstick tests. 20. Hyperglycemia first detected during pregnancy should be classified as gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes mellitus in pregnancy, based on WHO criteria. 21. In high-prevalence settings, provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) for HIV should be a routine component of antenatal care. In low-prevalence settings, PITC can be considered as part of efforts to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV and integrate testing with other key diagnostics. 22. Systematic screening for active tuberculosis (TB) should be considered for pregnant women in settings with a TB prevalence of 100/100,000 population or higher. 23. Clinical inquiry about intimate partner violence (IPV) should be strongly considered during antenatal care visits, provided there is capacity to offer supportive responses and referrals. 24. Health-care providers should ask all pregnant women about their tobacco use and exposure to second-hand smoke as early as possible in pregnancy and at every antenatal care visit. 25. Providers should also inquire about alcohol and substance use during pregnancy, as early as possible and at every antenatal care visit. 26. Replacing abdominal palpation with symphysis-fundal height (SFH) measurement for fetal growth assessment is not recommended to improve perinatal outcomes. Routine antenatal cardiotocography is also not recommended. 27. One ultrasound scan before 24 weeks of gestation is recommended to estimate gestational age, detect fetal anomalies and multiple pregnancies, reduce post-term labor induction, and improve the pregnancy experience. 28. Routine Doppler ultrasound examination of fetal blood vessels is not recommended to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. 29. A seven-day antibiotic regimen is recommended for pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) to prevent persistent bacteriuria and preterm birth.
